archetype.name: Super Bowl Contender (ground-and-defense)
archetype.definition: A team with the second-best net EPA in the league that wins by running the ball better than anyone and keeping opponents out of the end zone, not with Mahomes carrying the offense through the air.

report.headline: The league's best run game and a stingy defense, now with a patched line.
report.take:
These are not the Chiefs of 2018, when they led the league in offensive EPA and gave up points in bunches. The 2026 version looks more like 2023: an efficient team that leans on its defense and, this year, on a ground game. Kenneth Walker III has 120 carries, far more than anyone else, and the run offense ranks first in both EPA (0.075) and yards per carry (5.4). The line is a big part of that, with backs getting 2.9 yards before contact, fifth in the league. Mahomes has a passing offense that ranks only 14th in EPA. It is good enough, not the engine. A net EPA of 0.144, second in the league, says the 5-1 record is mostly real.

There is some help in the record. Kansas City leads the league in turnover margin at 1.2 a game, is perfect in one-score games, and the point differential implies 3.9 wins, not five. That luck is mild, though. Wins over expected is 1.08, ninth in the league, and it comes a year after the 2025 team finished 6-11 with the worst luck in the league: -4.4 wins over expected and 0.1 in one-score games. Some of that bad luck has swung back. The bigger change is the efficiency, with net EPA jumping from 0.05 to 0.144.

The defense is built to keep things in front of it. It ranks second against short passes, fourth in success rate allowed and second in red-zone touchdown rate (26.7%), and its tackling is clean. What it lacks is a pass rush. Eight sacks ranks 29th, and the defense is 21st in EPA allowed on deep passes. When a quarterback has time and pushes the ball downfield, this defense can be beaten. The Raiders threw for 365 yards in a three-point game.

The warning sign is the most recent game. In a 20-3 loss at Seattle, the passing offense posted -6 EPA and the team ran for 50 yards against the league's No. 2 defense. Now the line is thinner. Jaylon Moore, an 89%-snap tackle, is out with a concussion, Josh Simmons is on IR, and Rashee Rice is out again. A team whose identity is the run game and clean pockets has to show it can keep that identity with backups at tackle.

strengths.title: The league's most efficient run game
strengths.body: Kansas City ranks first in run EPA and yards per carry, sixth in run success, and its backs get 2.9 yards before contact. This is line play and design, not game script: the 220-yard day against Denver came in a game the Chiefs controlled, and four of six games went over 140 rushing yards. It should last as long as the interior holds, though the tackle injuries put that to the test.

strengths.title: A defense that wins the red zone
strengths.body: Opponents' drives tend to stall. The success rate allowed ranks fourth, short-pass EPA allowed second, and only 26.7% of red-zone trips end in touchdowns, second best. Points allowed per game ranks second, better than the yardage allowed (13th), so some of this is red-zone variance that could drift. Still, the tackling (missed tackles fifth) and the run defense are solid underneath it.

strengths.title: Clean pockets for Mahomes
strengths.body: Only 7 sacks allowed, the fewest in the league, and a pressure rate of 16.1% (fourth) keep the passing game on schedule even though it is not explosive. Some of that comes from Mahomes extending plays, but the line has earned it. With Moore and Simmons out, expect this to slip.

concerns.title: A middling passing game, now thinner
concerns.body: Passing EPA ranks 14th, and the game-by-game swings run from 13.4 against Indianapolis to -6 at Seattle. The targets are spread among Kelce, Worthy and Walker out of the backfield, and Rice, the most dynamic option, keeps missing time. Against good defenses, this passing game has not been able to take over a game when the run is shut down.

concerns.title: No pass rush, soft deep coverage
concerns.body: Eight sacks ranks 29th, the sack rate ranks 30th, and the defense is 21st in deep-pass EPA allowed. The coverage underneath is excellent, but quarterbacks who get time can find the big play over the top. This looks structural, not a slump: the pressure rate is only 19th.

concerns.title: Turnovers and special teams masking
concerns.body: A league-best turnover margin and a perfect record in one-score games have padded the record. Meanwhile special teams rank 28th, giving back field position every week. Turnover margins rarely hold at this level, and when they cool, the special-teams leak will cost close games.

trend.note: Five straight wins, built mostly on the run game and the defense, then a 20-3 dud at Seattle against the No. 2 defense. The passing offense has swung from week to week, but the team's overall level has held.

nextGame.headline: Walker against a leaky run defense, Mahomes against the league's sack leader.
nextGame.body:
The Book has Kansas City by 1.5 in Denver with a total of 41.5, a near coin flip between division leaders. Denver's 5-2 record runs well ahead of its play: net EPA ranks 14th, its luck ranks fifth, and it is perfect in one-score games. The Broncos win with defense. They rank fourth in EPA allowed, fourth against the pass and first in sacks with 21. Their offense ranks 23rd in EPA and 29th in success rate. Their weak spot is the run defense: 26th in rush EPA allowed, 28th in explosive runs allowed and last in missed tackles. The Chiefs exploited that in Week 1, running for 220 yards in a 31-10 win.

The injuries cut both ways. Kansas City is without tackle Jaylon Moore (concussion) and Josh Simmons (IR), right as it faces the league's best sack team, and Rashee Rice is out again. Denver is missing two starters in the secondary, Pat Surtain II and safety Talanoa Hufanga, has linebacker Jonah Elliss on IR, and lists Zach Allen (hamstring) and Jaylen Waddle (chest) as questionable. If Allen sits, Denver's pass rush loses a piece, and the matchup tilts toward Kansas City.

waysToWin.title: Run Walker into Denver's tackling problems
waysToWin.body: Denver ranks 26th in rush EPA allowed, 28th in explosive runs allowed and last in missed tackles. That is exactly what the league's best run offense wants to see. Leaning on the run also keeps Mahomes out of the obvious passing downs where Denver's rush wins. This is the same plan that produced 220 rushing yards in September.

waysToWin.title: Kelce against a depleted secondary
waysToWin.body: Denver ranks 29th in EPA allowed to tight ends, and it will be without Surtain and Hufanga. Kelce is tied for the team lead in targets. Quick throws to him and Walker get the ball out before the pass rush gets home and attack the coverage at its weakest.

waysToWin.title: Smother a punchless Denver offense
waysToWin.body: Denver ranks 30th in yards per game and 29th in success rate. Kansas City's defense excels at forcing long fields and holding in the red zone. If the Chiefs win early downs, they can keep this game in the teens and protect a small lead.

waysToLose.title: Denver's rush beats the backup tackles
waysToLose.body: Denver leads the league with 21 sacks and ranks second in QB hit rate. Kansas City will face that rush without Moore, an 89%-snap tackle, and without Simmons. If early downs go wrong and Mahomes faces third-and-long, this could look like the Seattle game.

waysToLose.title: Lose the hidden-yardage game
waysToLose.body: With a total of 41.5, field position and turnovers will decide it. Kansas City's special teams rank 28th. Denver's 11 takeaways tie the Chiefs for third, and the Broncos are perfect in close games too. A short field off a turnover or a return could be enough.

waysToLose.title: Bo Nix gets time to go deep
waysToLose.body: Kansas City barely gets home (sack rate 30th) and is 21st against deep passes. Denver's quarterback holds the ball longer than most (time to throw ranks eighth). A couple of completions over the top could swing a game the Broncos cannot win by moving the ball methodically.

nextGame.watch: Whether Kansas City's patched tackle spots can handle Denver's pass rush on early downs. If they hold up, the run game should control the game.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation should hold up: a top run game, a sound defense, and an efficiency profile that ranks second in the league. The turnover margin will come back toward normal, and the perfect record in close games will not last, so expect a couple of losses that were wins in the first six weeks. The schedule has a soft stretch right after Denver (the Jets, Atlanta, Arizona). Then it turns hard, with Buffalo, the Rams and Cincinnati on the road and San Francisco at home in December.

What separates this team from a regular-season winner and a true contender is the passing game. Mahomes is working with a passing offense that ranks only 14th, Rice keeps missing time and the line is banged up. If the tackles return around the Thanksgiving estimates and Rice gets healthy, Kansas City has a ceiling near the top of the AFC. If not, it is a very good team that struggles against elite defenses, as it did at Seattle.
swingFactors: Return of Moore and Simmons at tackle
How fast the turnover margin cools

confidence.note: Six games of strong efficiency, but the line injuries and an uneven passing game add uncertainty.
